cues.text: A Wanderer Who Could Not Stay Settled
Cronan was born in the territory of Ely O'Carroll in Ireland, the son of a man named Odhran, and spent his younger years in Connacht before returning to his native district around the year 610.
What the surviving accounts remember most vividly about his early monastic life is his restlessness.
He is said to have founded and then given away as many as fifty dwellings, one after another.

He handed each to a needier hermit before moving on to build the next—a pattern less of instability than deliberate refusal to let any single possession, even a modest hermit's cell, take root in him.
Settling at Roscrea
Cronan eventually settled at Seanross, a wooded and desolate spot so remote that pilgrims seeking him routinely became lost trying to find it.
Recognizing that such isolation suited his own temperament but could not sustain a lasting community, he relocated to Roscrea.
There, he founded the monastery and school that would carry his name for centuries afterward, drawing students and monks from across the region.
A Gospel Book and a Legendary Feast
Cronan is remembered in particular for commissioning an illuminated copy of the four Gospels for use at Roscrea, produced by a monk named Dimma.
The manuscript survives today as the Book of Dimma, one of the treasured illuminated Gospel books of early medieval Ireland.
It was later housed in a gilded case commissioned by a twelfth-century lord of the region.
Later tradition, warmer than historically verifiable, also credits Cronan with a more lighthearted miracle.

Finding himself short of drink for a gathering of guests, he is said to have prayed and obtained, by divine favor, so generous a supply of beer that the whole company left thoroughly and cheerfully inebriated.
The story clearly meant to illustrate a hospitality as generous as his earlier habit of giving away his own dwellings.
Blindness and Death
Toward the end of his life Cronan lost his sight, continuing to govern his monastery and school in blindness until his death, which the most reliable ancient reckoning places around the year 640.
His feast has been kept on April 28 in Irish calendars ever since, and Roscrea itself, the small Tipperary town his monastery gave rise to, still claims him as its patron.
Legacy

Cronan's story survives less through hard documentary record than through the affectionate, sometimes clearly embellished memory of the community he founded — a caution any clear-eyed telling of his life must carry throughout.
What comes through even so is a monk who treated hospitality, and the refusal to be tied down by any possession however small, as a kind of asceticism in its own right.
We recognize in Cronan a reminder that generosity, freely and repeatedly given away, can be as demanding a discipline as any fast.
A life spent handing things over to others, again and again, is its own quiet form of holiness.
